ABSTRACT
Recent interest in the external validity of prediction models (i.e., the problem of different train and
test distributions, known asdataset shift) has produced many methods for ﬁnding predictive distribu-
tions that are invariant to dataset shifts and can be used for prediction in new, unseen environments.
However, these methods consider different types of shifts and have been developed under disparate
frameworks, making it difﬁcult to theoretically analyze how solutions differ with respect to stability
and accuracy. Taking a causal graphical view, we use a ﬂexible graphical representation to express
various types of dataset shifts. Given a known graph of the data generating process, we show that
all invariant distributions correspond to a causal hierarchy of graphical operators which disable the
edges in the graph that are responsible for the shifts. The hierarchy provides a common theoreti-
cal underpinning for understanding when and how stability to shifts can be achieved, and in what
ways stable distributions can differ. We use it to establish conditions for minimax optimal perfor-
mance across environments, and derive new algorithms that ﬁnd optimal stable distributions. Using
this new perspective, we empirically demonstrate that that there is a tradeoff between minimax and
average performance.

summary: Recent interest in the external validity of prediction models (i.e., the problem of different train and test distributions, known as dataset shift) has produced many methods for finding predictive distributions that are invariant to dataset shifts and can be used for prediction in new, unseen environments. However, these methods consider different types of shifts and have been developed under disparate frameworks, making it difficult to theoretically analyze how solutions differ with respect to stability and accuracy. Taking a causal graphical view, we use a flexible graphical representation to express various types of dataset shifts. Given a known graph of the data generating process, we show that all invariant distributions correspond to a causal hierarchy of graphical operators which disable the edges in the graph that are responsible for the shifts. Title:
Objectivity, basis ambiguity, and the classical simulability of concordant quantum computation
Authors:
Bishal Kumar Das
,
Sourav Manna
,
Vaibhav Madhok
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract:
Concordant quantum computations, in which circuits whose register carries zero quantum discord with respect to every subsystem at every step, contain neither entanglement nor any other form of quantum correlation, yet no efficient classical simulation of them is known beyond restricted gate sets. We argue that the obstruction is not a shortage of correlations but the absence of a uniquely identifiable local product basis, and we develop this \emph{basis ambiguity} on two fronts. Quantitatively, we introduce the Basis Ambiguity Measure $\beta\in[0,1]$, the normalized dimension of the manifold of admissible diagonalizing bases on a gate support, and prove a sharp equivalence: a concordance-preserving gate that defeats the Local Basis Finder of Cable and Browne exists if and only if $\beta>0$. Both directions are constructive. Physically, we identify the resource whose absence the obstruction is: \emph{basis objectivity}, a redundant and independently accessible record of the local basis. We show that an environment in spectrum broadcast form, together with the system--environment interaction map, replaces the NP-hard degeneracy test of Eastin by a fixed number of pairwise fragment comparisons per gate, at a cost independent of register size and circuit depth; the two ingredients live on different axes (state and dynamics), and neither alone suffices. We further prove that a theory in which every state has a strictly unique decomposition into perfectly distinguishable pure states has a simplex state space and lacks the continuity content of Hardy's fifth axiom, so that $\beta$ is a computational witness of that axiom. Finally, as a proof of principle that basis ambiguity carries operational content, we present a concordant encryption protocol with hidden local bases, together with an explicit account of what its security does and does not rest on.
